paragraphs.simple: Now they must find four special kinds of writing for Morgan's library. This will help save Camelot.

paragraphs.simple: It is a dark, sad-looking Sunday. Jack looks out of the window and wonders when the tree house will come back.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, guess what!” Annie said. She charged into Jack’s room.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs into Jack's room. She saw a light in the woods. She thinks it was the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “Bring your backpack, just in case!” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack to bring his bag, because they may need it. Jack is always glad to look for the tree house.

paragraphs.context: The woods were dark under the storm clouds. A cool wind shook the leaves.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run into the dark woods.
paragraphs.simple: It is dark in the woods because of the storm clouds. A cool wind moves the leaves.

paragraphs.context: The magic tree house stood out against the gray sky.
paragraphs.simple: They can see the tree house clearly in front of the grey sky. Annie was right.

paragraphs.context: Camelot is in trouble. To save the kingdom
paragraphs.simple: Morgan writes that Camelot is in danger. They must find four special kinds of writing for her library.

paragraphs.context: “Camelot is in trouble?” said Jack. “What’s that mean?”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They do not understand the danger.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks what Morgan means. Annie does not know, but she wants to hurry and find the first writing.

paragraphs.context: On the cover was a painting of a peaceful-looking field and a blue sky.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book is about the Civil War.
paragraphs.simple: The book has a picture of a quiet field. Its title is The Civil War.

paragraphs.context: “Cool?” she said. “War’s not cool.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks war is exciting, but Annie says war is not fun at all.

paragraphs.context: “It sort of is,” Jack said uncomfortably.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks war is a bit like a game.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows war is bad, but he thinks some parts of it are fun, like a game. He will learn that he is wrong.
paragraphs.tone: Jack feels a little bad as he says it.

paragraphs.context: Glaring sunlight filled the tree house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They arrive on a hot day.
paragraphs.simple: Very bright, hot sunlight comes into the tree house.

paragraphs.context: Their clothes had magically been changed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They wear clothes from long ago.
paragraphs.simple: Magic changed their clothes. Annie has a long dress. Jack has rough trousers, a shirt with long sleeves and an old leather bag.

background.note: A knapsack is an old kind of backpack, often made of leather or cloth.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw a soldier riding a horse out of the woods.
paragraphs.simple: A soldier rides out of the woods. His horse is muddy, his blue uniform is torn and his arm is bleeding.

paragraphs.context: Another man rode into the field.
paragraphs.simple: Another soldier comes. His uniform is old and torn, and he has a bandage around his head. (The book prints "ban-daged" with a hyphen, so the reader sees two pieces, "ban" and "daged". Read it as "bandaged".)

paragraphs.context: because it was fought between the Southern and Northern states of the United States.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Civil War: North against South.
paragraphs.simple: The war was between the Southern and Northern states. Southern soldiers wore grey and were called Confederates. Northern soldiers wore blue and were called Union soldiers.

background.note: Another name for the American Civil War, because the states of one country fought each other.
The Confederate States were 11 Southern states that left the USA in 1861.
"The Union" means the United States, the Northern side that wanted to keep the country together.

paragraphs.context: “So they’re Union soldiers,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The soldiers wear blue, so they are from the North. Jack writes in his notebook. (In this e-book, Jack's notes are pictures, so no text comes after "wrote:".)

paragraphs.context: The Civil War was a cruel and bloody war.
paragraphs.simple: More Americans died in the Civil War than in all other American wars together. One young man in every five died or was hurt.

paragraphs.context: They all looked sad and weary. Some of them limped.
paragraphs.simple: The soldiers are sad and very tired. Some walk badly because they are hurt. One man falls down.

paragraphs.context: She was holding her hand out to the fallen soldier.
paragraphs.simple: Annie gives the soldier her hand and helps him stand up. She walks next to him.

paragraphs.context: The sun was scorching hot as Jack ran through the dry field.
paragraphs.simple: The sun is very, very hot. Jack is wet with sweat in his rough clothes. He walks with Annie and the soldiers.

paragraphs.context: At the edge of the field was a steep hill.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see a camp of tents.
paragraphs.simple: From the top of the hill they see rows and rows of white tents. A soldier is very glad: "We're saved."

paragraphs.context: Outside one tent was a long line of men in torn blue uniforms.
paragraphs.simple: Many tired, hurt soldiers wait in a line. Some can hardly stand. Women give them food and water.

paragraphs.context: During the Civil War, field hospitals were set up quickly near battlefields
paragraphs.simple: Field hospitals were made quickly near battles. Hurt soldiers stayed there for a short time. This one cared for more than 400 sick and hurt men.

background.note: Virginia is a state in the east of the USA. Many Civil War battles were fought there.

paragraphs.context: More than 3,000 women helped out as nurses during the Civil War.
paragraphs.simple: Before the war only men were nurses. In the war, more than 3,000 women helped as nurses.

paragraphs.context: Jack wanted to find the special writing for Morgan and go home.
paragraphs.simple: The sad place makes Jack feel sick. He wants to find the writing quickly and go home.

paragraphs.context: Waves of heat rose from a small cooking fire.
paragraphs.simple: A young nurse is making coffee over a fire. It is hot and there are flies everywhere.

paragraphs.context: Her face was red and beaded with sweat.
paragraphs.simple: Her face is red and covered with drops of sweat. Her eyes look very, very tired.

paragraphs.context: “Frog Creek,” said Annie. “We’d like to volunteer as nurses.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they want to help as nurses for no money. The nurse is not surprised at all.

paragraphs.context: “We could certainly use some help,” she said, sighing.
paragraphs.simple: The nurses would be glad of help. Some have not slept for days.

paragraphs.context: “The wounded are coming here from a battle near Richmond,”
paragraphs.simple: Hurt soldiers keep coming from a battle. It seems that it will never stop.

background.note: Richmond, in Virginia, was the capital city of the Confederate (Southern) states. There were many battles near it.

paragraphs.context: “Just try to give them comfort,” the nurse said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The nurse asks them to comfort the men.
paragraphs.simple: The nurse wants them to make the men feel better. She has no time to explain, so she gives them a list.

paragraphs.context: Lessen sorrow and give hope.
paragraphs.simple: Make sadness smaller and help people hope for good things.

paragraphs.context: Put aside your own feelings.
paragraphs.simple: Do not think about your own feelings. Think about the other person.

paragraphs.context: “Follow that list,” said the nurse, “and you can’t go wrong.”
paragraphs.simple: If they do what the list says, they will not make mistakes.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t you get it?” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands: the list is "something to follow". It is the special writing for Morgan!

paragraphs.context: The truth was that he didn’t want to help.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid of the sad tent.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not really want to help. It is too sad to be with hurt and suffering soldiers.

paragraphs.context: Jack groaned. He knew he couldn’t change her mind.
paragraphs.simple: Jack knows Annie will not change her plan. He reads the first rule: be cheerful.

paragraphs.context: The scene inside was like a nightmare.
paragraphs.simple: Inside the tent it is like a very bad dream.

paragraphs.context: The tent was hot and stuffy.
paragraphs.simple: The tent is hot with no fresh air. Twelve hurt soldiers lie on small beds. They ask for food and water or make sounds of pain.

paragraphs.context: Jack wanted to rush back outside.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to run out. But Annie starts working at once. She smiles and is cheerful.

paragraphs.context: Keeping his eyes down, Jack handed the cup to the patient.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not look at the men. He feels shy and does not know what to say.

paragraphs.context: Just like the last tent, it was filled with wounded soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: The next tent is full of hurt soldiers too. All of them are African-Americans.

background.note: About 180,000 African-American soldiers fought for the Union in the Civil War. Many of them had been slaves.

paragraphs.context: “Thank you for your kindness, son,” the soldier said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: An old soldier speaks to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: An old soldier thanks Jack. He calls Jack "son" in a friendly way.

paragraphs.context: “No. I’ll never be with my family again,” he said quietly.
paragraphs.simple: The man says he will never see his family again. His wife and children were sold long ago.

paragraphs.context: “All of us in this tent were once slaves,” the man said.
paragraphs.simple: All the men in the tent were slaves before. They ran away from their owners in the South to fight to end slavery. This man ran 30 miles with no shoes to warn the Union army.

background.note: Before the Civil War, millions of African-Americans in the South were slaves. Their owners could buy and sell them, and even sell their children.

paragraphs.context: “You’re a very brave freedom fighter,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the man is very brave. He fought so that his people could be free.

paragraphs.context: He found a picture of African-Americans standing on a platform.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees a picture of men, women and children in chains, standing up high so that people could buy them.

paragraphs.context: In the 1800s, the United States was divided over the issue of slavery.
paragraphs.simple: The North wanted to end slavery. The South wanted to keep slaves to work on its big farms. This disagreement caused the Civil War.

background.note: Plantations were very big farms in the South. Slaves grew cotton, tobacco and rice there.

paragraphs.context: “One day your great-great-grandchildren will be doctors and lawyers,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells the man about the future: his family will be doctors, lawyers, leaders and teachers.

paragraphs.context: “Can you see the future, son?” he asked.
paragraphs.simple: The man asks if Jack can see the future. Jack says "in a way", because he comes from the future. The man smiles a beautiful smile.

paragraphs.context: A horse-drawn wagon was barreling into the camp.
paragraphs.simple: A wagon pulled by horses comes very fast into the camp. People shout that Clara Barton is back.

paragraphs.context: “Who’s Clara Barton?” asked Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has heard her name, but he does not remember who she is. Annie is surprised he does not know.

background.note: Clara Barton (1821 to 1912) was a famous nurse in the Civil War. Later she started the American Red Cross.

paragraphs.context: Clara Barton was a famous Civil War nurse.
paragraphs.simple: Clara Barton used her own money for medicine and bandages. She drove her wagon onto the battlefield to save hurt soldiers. People called her the "Angel of the Battlefield".

background.note: Soldiers gave Clara Barton this name because she came to help them in the middle of the fighting.
Her "ambulance" was a wagon pulled by horses. There were no cars then.

paragraphs.context: She doesn’t look like an angel, Jack thought.
paragraphs.simple: Clara is very small, with a simple, serious face. Her dark hair is tied at the back. She wears black clothes.

paragraphs.context: “First, you can call me Clara,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Clara is friendly. She asks them to ride with her toward the battlefield to get more hurt men.

paragraphs.context: Jack didn’t want to admit he was afraid.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not want to say that he is afraid, so he says, "Sure, no problem."

paragraphs.context: She snapped the reins.
paragraphs.simple: Clara moves the straps quickly, and the horses go. The wagon makes clouds of dust.

paragraphs.context: The wagon jerked and swayed as it bumped over the dry ground.
paragraphs.simple: The wagon moves roughly over the dry ground. It is very hot and dusty.

paragraphs.context: The boom of cannons grew louder and louder.
paragraphs.simple: The big guns get louder. Jack hears small popping sounds too, like firecrackers.

paragraphs.context: Jack remembered that muskets were long, old-fashioned guns.
paragraphs.simple: Muskets were long guns used long ago. They are making the popping sound.

background.note: A Civil War soldier's musket fired one bullet at a time. It took about 20 seconds to load it again.

paragraphs.context: “Cannon shells exploding,” said Clara Barton.
paragraphs.simple: Shells are like small bombs. They blow up and have ruined a lot of farm land.

background.note: Civil War cannons fired metal balls and shells. Their boom could be heard many miles away.

paragraphs.context: Jack squinted at the passing countryside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The land is full of holes.
paragraphs.simple: The ground has ugly holes, and long narrow holes are cut through the fields.

paragraphs.context: “No. Those are trenches the soldiers dug for a battle,” Clara said.
paragraphs.simple: Soldiers dig long holes to hide in. They sit there every day and shoot at each other.

background.note: In the Civil War, soldiers dug trenches near cities like Petersburg, Virginia, and lived in them for months.

paragraphs.context: She drove the wagon to a narrow creek.
paragraphs.simple: Clara drives to a small river. The wagon stops. Then Jack hears a high whistling sound.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt a rush of panic.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is suddenly very frightened. His hands shake as he reads the rule: be brave.

paragraphs.context: Another cannon shell whizzed overhead, then another.
paragraphs.simple: Shells fly over their heads. The ground blows up in flashes of light. Earth and smoke fly everywhere. The horses make frightened sounds.

paragraphs.context: The firing came to an end.
paragraphs.simple: The shooting stops. The horses become quiet. The smoke goes away.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s legs felt wobbly as he followed Annie to the creek.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's legs shake after the fear. They fill the water bottles and get back into the wagon.

paragraphs.context: The man looked very young, more like a teenage boy.
paragraphs.simple: The hurt man is very young, like a teenager. His uniform is grey: he is a Confederate soldier.

paragraphs.context: “When someone is hurt, you give them a helping hand, no matter who they are,”
paragraphs.simple: Clara says you must help everyone who is hurt, from either side. Good and brave people are on both sides. War is not simple.

paragraphs.context: They came across more ragged men resting in the shade of an oak tree.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Union soldiers rest under a tree.
paragraphs.simple: They find more soldiers in torn clothes resting under a tree. These soldiers wear blue.

paragraphs.context: “Can a Confederate and a Union soldier be together?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack is worried that the two sides cannot be in the same wagon.

paragraphs.context: “Sometimes men are simply too sick and tired to be enemies anymore,”
paragraphs.simple: Clara says some men are too sick and tired to be enemies. Some even know each other. The war has broken many families and friendships.

background.note: In the Civil War, brothers and cousins sometimes fought on different sides.

paragraphs.context: “Only John, our drummer boy,” a soldier said.
paragraphs.simple: Only John, the boy who plays the drum, needs to go to hospital. He is ill from the heat.

background.note: Heat stroke is very dangerous. The body gets too hot and cannot cool down.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, Jack!” whispered Annie. “He looks just like you.”
paragraphs.simple: The drummer boy looks a lot like Jack, but a few years older.

paragraphs.context: The drummer boy moved as if he were walking in his sleep.
paragraphs.simple: John walks as if he is asleep. His head hangs down and his feet move slowly in the dust. The soldiers ask them to look after him.

paragraphs.context: “He does have heat stroke,” Clara said.
paragraphs.simple: Clara says both boys are very ill. They must get to the hospital fast. Jack and Annie must help.

paragraphs.context: “Gently press these cloths against their faces to help cool them off,”
paragraphs.simple: Clara gives them wet cloths to put softly on the boys' faces, to make them less hot.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie gently patted the soldiers’ faces with the damp cloths.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that the two young men are more the same than different.

paragraphs.context: In another time and place, they might have been friends, Jack thought.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks that if there were no war, the two boys could be friends.

paragraphs.context: “Try to bring down his fever,” Clara said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clara asks them to stay with John.
paragraphs.simple: Clara wants them to make John's body less hot with ice. They must tell her when his fever is lower.

paragraphs.context: Jack wrapped some ice in a rag.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts ice in cloth and presses it on John. Annie moves the air to make him cooler and to keep the flies away.

paragraphs.context: The Civil War was the last war to use drummer boys.
paragraphs.simple: Drums told soldiers when to eat, how to walk and how to fight. In the smoke, the drum helped soldiers find each other.

background.note: Some drummer boys in the Civil War were only 10 or 12 years old.

paragraphs.context: “No! No!” the boy said. He sounded frantic.
paragraphs.simple: John is very upset. He says he must go back to the battle, because the soldiers need his drum.

paragraphs.context: Put aside your own feelings, he remembered.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers the rule. He tells John he can go back when he is better.

paragraphs.context: “Jack!” said Annie. “He’ll get hurt or killed!
paragraphs.simple: Annie is afraid John will be killed. Jack is afraid too, but he says they must put their own feelings aside.

paragraphs.context: “You know, you’re the bravest kid I’ve ever met,” Jack said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says John is the bravest boy he knows. John says Jack looks like his little brother.

paragraphs.context: “You look just like my big brother,” said Jack
paragraphs.simple: Jack says John looks like a big brother, but then remembers he has no brothers. They all laugh.

paragraphs.context: It was strange. Jack hardly knew the drummer boy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has only just met John, but he feels like his brother.

paragraphs.context: Listening to the cannon fire in the distance, Jack was afraid for the boy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears the guns and is afraid for John. Will he live to see his family?

paragraphs.context: Bright lights flashed against the dark blue horizon
paragraphs.simple: Far away, bright lights show where shells are exploding.

paragraphs.context: “Every time you see a flash, you know a shell may have taken a life or many lives,”
paragraphs.simple: Clara says each flash may kill one or many people.

paragraphs.context: “A whole world can vanish in that flash
paragraphs.mainIdea: A life can end in a moment.
paragraphs.simple: In one flash, everything in a young man's life can end: his happiness, his sadness and his memories.

paragraphs.context: “All wars are cruel,” said Clara Barton.
paragraphs.simple: People think they must fight for ideas they believe in. But war is not about being famous or great. It is about terrible pain and sadness.

paragraphs.context: “It makes me miss my mom and dad,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The war makes Annie want to be with her parents. She is tired and sad. She is not cheerful any more.

paragraphs.context: Jack thought of all the wounded men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not want to give up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks of the hurt men who need help. He says they must stay, because the list says "Don't give up."

paragraphs.context: “Oh, yes,” she said, nodding.
paragraphs.simple: Clara sees that a nurse wrote down the things she often says. She adds one more: do not forget the people who love you.

paragraphs.context: “Of course,” said Clara.
paragraphs.simple: Clara says yes. Her words help in all of life, not only in a hospital.

paragraphs.context: The sun was setting as they walked out of the camp.
paragraphs.simple: The sun goes down. Guns boom far away. Soldiers sing a song around a fire.

paragraphs.context: We’re tenting tonight
paragraphs.simple: The song says: we are sleeping in tents tonight in the old camp.

background.note: "Tenting Tonight on the Old Camp Ground" is a real song from the Civil War. Soldiers on both sides sang it.

paragraphs.context: Give us a song to cheer
paragraphs.simple: Sing us a song to make our tired hearts happier.

paragraphs.context: But the soldiers’ song still carried through the warm, starry night.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot see anything, but he can still hear the song.

paragraphs.context: Wishing for the war to cease …
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldiers want the war to end.
paragraphs.simple: Many hearts are tired. They wish the war would stop.

paragraphs.context: As Jack listened, he thought of Clara Barton, the elderly slave
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks of all the people he met: Clara, the old soldier, the young Southern soldier and John.

paragraphs.context: “War is not a game,” Jack said softly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack now knows that war is not a game at all. Before, he thought parts of it were fun.

paragraphs.context: To see the dawn of peace.
paragraphs.simple: The soldiers hope to see the start of peace.

paragraphs.context: There was a booming in the distance.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears booming. For a moment he thinks they are still in the war.

paragraphs.context: They were home. They were back in the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: They are home again in their own clothes. The booming is only thunder, and Jack loves it.

paragraphs.context: “Wait. Leave the list in the tree house,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They leave the list for Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says to leave the list for Morgan. It is the first special writing.

paragraphs.context: “But you know what’s weird about getting that list?
paragraphs.mainIdea: They had to live the list.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks they could not just take the list home. They had to do what it says first. Jack thinks she is right.

paragraphs.context: She picked a piece of paper off the tree house floor.
paragraphs.simple: Another note says: come back on Wednesday. That is when they will look for the next writing.

paragraphs.context: “Dad! Mom!” Annie cried. “We’re so glad to see you!”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are glad to see their parents.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is very happy to see her parents. Their father does not understand why.

paragraphs.context: “One of your great-great-great-grandfathers was a drummer boy.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: A drummer boy in their family!
paragraphs.simple: Their dad says one of their grandfathers from long ago was a drummer boy.

paragraphs.context: “No, he grew up to be a schoolteacher,” their mom said.
paragraphs.simple: John was not hurt in the war. He became a teacher and had five children. Jack and Annie shout for joy.

paragraphs.context: As Jack hurried up to his room, some words from the Civil War song ran through his mind:
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks of the song again: a song to make tired hearts happy, a song of home.

paragraphs.context: 1) More soldiers were killed in the Civil War than in any other war in American history.
paragraphs.simple: The Civil War killed more American soldiers than any other war.

paragraphs.context: 2) In 1861, when the Civil War began, about 3.5 million people were slaves in the South.
paragraphs.simple: When the war started, about 3.5 million people in the South were slaves.

paragraphs.context: 3) In 1865, President Abraham Lincoln convinced Congress to pass the 13th Amendment
paragraphs.simple: In 1865, a new law ended slavery in all of the USA.

background.note: Abraham Lincoln was President of the USA during the Civil War. He was killed in 1865, just after the war ended.
The 13th Amendment is the change to the US Constitution that ended slavery.

paragraphs.context: 4) Eleven states fought for the Confederacy.
paragraphs.simple: Eleven states fought for the South. Twenty-three states fought for the North (the Union), and some other lands too.

background.note: Territories were parts of the USA that were not yet states, like Colorado and Nebraska in 1861.

paragraphs.context: 5) Soldiers during the Civil War often sang songs together.
paragraphs.simple: Soldiers often sang together. The song in this book is a real, famous song from 1861.

background.note: Walter Kittredge was an American singer. He wrote this song during the Civil War, at the time he was called to join the army.

paragraphs.context: nursed soldiers during the Civil War. She also used her own money
paragraphs.simple: Clara Barton was a nurse in the Civil War. She bought things for soldiers with her own money. After the war, she helped more than 22,000 families get news of missing soldiers.

paragraphs.context: In 1881, Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross.
paragraphs.simple: In 1881, Clara Barton started the American Red Cross. It helps people in wars and after big storms and floods.

paragraphs.context: It is thought that nearly 60,000 boys served as drummer boys
paragraphs.simple: About 60,000 boys played drums or bugles for the armies in the Civil War. Johnny Clem joined at 11 and became a sergeant at 13.

a number of.example: A number of territories also fought for the Union.

afraid for.meaning: Worried that something bad will happen to someone.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as if.example: he swayed as if he were about to faint.

as soon as.meaning: At the moment when; right after.
as soon as.example: You can go back as soon as you feel better.

as though.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as though.example: Jack felt as though he were frying in the hot sunlight.

at once.example: We must get them to the hospital at once.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: They are about to set off

be supposed to.meaning: Should do something, because someone said so or because it is the plan.

bring down.meaning: To make something lower. "Bring down his fever" means make his body less hot.
bring down.example: Try to bring down his fever

calm down.meaning: To become calm, not excited or afraid.

catch up with.meaning: To come up to someone who is in front of you, by going faster.
catch up with.example: he hurried to catch up with Annie.

catch your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment because you are surprised; or to rest until you can breathe normally again.

change your mind.meaning: To make a different choice from before.
change your mind.example: He knew he couldn’t change her mind.

come across.meaning: To find or meet someone by chance.
come across.example: They came across more ragged men

come to a halt.example: The wagon came to a halt.

come to an end.example: The firing came to an end.

cool off.meaning: To become, or make someone, less hot.

could use.meaning: "We could use some help" means we would like some help, because we need it.
could use.example: We could certainly use some help

day after day.meaning: Every day, for a long time.
day after day.example: Day after day, they sit in the trenches

do without.meaning: To manage when you do not have someone or something.

drummer boy.meaning: A boy who played the drum in an army long ago.

fall silent.meaning: To stop talking and become quiet.

field hospital.meaning: A hospital in tents near a battlefield.
field hospital.example: During the Civil War, field hospitals were set up quickly

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: “I guess we’ll find out,” said Annie.

forget it.meaning: "Forget it" means "No, that is not possible. Stop thinking about it."

get it.meaning: 1. To understand. "Don't you get it?" means "Don't you understand?" (Friendly talk.) 2. To receive something.

get ready.meaning: To make yourself ready for something.
get ready.example: So now get ready for your next daring reading adventure

get to work.example: But Annie got right to work.

give out.meaning: To give something to each person in a group.
give out.example: Women wearing dark dresses were giving out food and water

go hungry.example: the patients in the next tent will go hungry and thirsty

go on.meaning: 1. To keep talking after stopping. 2. To go on an adventure or a trip = to go and do it.

go wrong.meaning: To make a mistake. "You can't go wrong" means you will not make a mistake.

grow up.example: he grew up to be a schoolteacher

guess what.meaning: "Guess what!" is what you say before you tell someone surprising news.

had better.meaning: Should. "We better hurry" means we should hurry. (In friendly talk, people often leave out "had".)
had better.example: But we better hurry and find these writings.

hand out.meaning: 1. To give something to each person in a group. 2. "Hold your hand out" = reach your hand toward someone.
hand out.example: She handed out pieces of bread

hand over.example: as he handed over the last cup

hear from.meaning: To get a letter, call or message from someone.
hear from.example: the readers I meet and hear from

heat stroke.meaning: An illness that comes from being too hot for too long. You may feel very weak or faint.

heave a sigh.meaning: To breathe out a long, loud sigh, because you are tired or unhappy.

help out.meaning: To help, especially when there is a lot of work.
help out.example: More than 3,000 women helped out as nurses during the Civil War.

help someone to their feet.example: She helped him to his feet.

helping hand.meaning: Help. "Give someone a helping hand" means help them.
helping hand.example: you give them a helping hand

home sweet home.meaning: "Home, sweet home" means "It is so good to be home."

ice pack.meaning: A bag or cloth with ice in it, that you press on your body to make it cold.
ice pack.example: A nurse will give you ice packs

in a way.meaning: In some way, but not completely.

in case.meaning: Because something might happen. "Just in case" means because we might need it.
in case.example: “Bring your backpack, just in case!” she said.

in rags.example: His blue uniform was in rags, too.

in trouble.meaning: In a bad or dangerous situation.

keep going.meaning: To not stop; to go on.

known as.meaning: Called by a name. "She became known as the Angel" means people started to call her that.
known as.example: she became known as the “Angel of the Battlefield.”

lead to.example: This disagreement between the North and South led to the Civil War.

live to see.meaning: To live long enough to see something happen.
live to see.example: Will he live to see his family again?

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look at something. 2. To find a word or fact in a book.
look up.example: Jack looked up from his notebook.

more and more.meaning: A bigger and bigger number or amount.

move on.meaning: To go on to the next place or person.
move on.example: Jack moved on to the next patient

no matter.meaning: "No matter who they are" means it is not important who they are.

no problem.meaning: "No problem" means "Yes, I can do that easily."

not at all.meaning: Not in any way. "She didn't seem at all surprised" means she did not seem surprised.
not at all.example: The young woman didn’t seem at all surprised.

one another.example: firing their muskets at one another.

out of every.meaning: "One out of every five" means one in every group of five.
out of every.example: One out of every five young men in the nation died or was wounded.

over and over.example: The ground exploded over and over in flashes of light.

pass out.meaning: To give something to each person in a group.
pass out.example: Soon Jack and Annie had finished passing out food and water.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up from the floor or a table. 2. To go and get someone and take them somewhere.
pick up.example: There are more wounded waiting to be picked up.

point of view.meaning: The way you see or think about something.
point of view.example: If you could see the world from my point of view

pour down.meaning: When rain pours down, a lot of rain falls very fast.
pour down.example: the rain began to pour down.

put aside.meaning: To not think about something for a time. "Put aside your own feelings" means do not think about how you feel.

put together.meaning: Added together. "More than all the other wars put together" means more than all the other wars added together.
put together.example: More people died in this war than in all of America’s other wars put together.

right away.example: We better get him to Clara’s ambulance right away

roll up.meaning: To fold your sleeves up your arms. "Roll up your sleeves" also means get ready to work hard.
roll up.example: She rolled up her sleeves and smiled.

run away.meaning: To leave a place secretly or quickly to escape.
run away.example: We ran away from our owners in the South

run through your mind.meaning: When words or a song run through your mind, you keep thinking of them.
run through your mind.example: some words from the Civil War song ran through his mind

set off.example: They are about to set off to find the first of these

set up.meaning: To build or put something in place, ready to use.
set up.example: field hospitals were set up quickly near battlefields

side by side.example: Jack looked at the young men lying side by side.

sort of.meaning: A little; in some way. (Friendly talk.)
sort of.example: “It sort of is,” Jack said uncomfortably.

stand out.meaning: To be easy to see because it is different from what is around it.
stand out.example: The magic tree house stood out against the gray sky.

take a life.example: a shell may have taken a life or many lives

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.example: This field hospital in Virginia took care of over 400 patients.

tear apart.meaning: To make people angry with each other and break up a family or friendship.
tear apart.example: Many families and friendships have been torn apart by this war.

thank goodness.meaning: "Thank goodness!" means "I am so glad!" You say it when something bad has stopped or did not happen.
thank goodness.example: “Thank goodness,” said the soldier beside Jack.

time and space.example: She travels through time and space, gathering books.

with a heavy heart.example: With a heavy heart, Jack stepped out

write down.meaning: To write something on paper so that you do not forget it.
write down.example: I see one of my nurses has written down the things I often say.

oh man.meaning: Something you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid or happy. "Oh, man!" is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a real man.

oh brother.meaning: "Oh, brother!" is something you say when you feel a little tired of something or annoyed.

oh great.meaning: Said in an unhappy way, "Oh, great" means "Oh, no! This is bad!"
oh great.example: Be brave. Oh, great, he thought.
